source.text: זְב֣וּבֵי מָ֔וֶת יַבְאִ֥ישׁ יַבִּ֖יעַ שֶׁ֣מֶן רוֹקֵ֑חַ יָקָ֛ר מֵחָכְמָ֥ה מִכָּב֖וֹד סִכְל֥וּת מְעָֽט׃

records.literal_gloss: Flies of death make stink, make bubble [the] oil of [a] perfumer; weightier than wisdom, than honor, [is] folly a little.

en.L: Flies of death make the oil of [the] perfumer stink [and] ferment; \q a little folly [is] weightier than wisdom, than honor.
en.B: Dead flies make the perfumer's oil stink and go bad; \q so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
en.R: A few dead flies can make fine perfume smell bad. \q In the same way, a little foolishness can outweigh wisdom and honor.

decisions.choice: flies of death: dead flies
decisions.reason: "Flies of death" most likely means flies that have died in the oil. Some read "deadly flies", flies that bring disease. The picture is the same: something small spoils something precious.

decisions.choice: the perfumer's oil: costly scented oil prepared by a skilled maker
decisions.reason: Perfumers blended spices into oil for anointing (Exodus 30:25, 35). Such oil was precious (7:1), and a few dead flies would ruin a whole jar.

decisions.choice: a little folly is weightier than wisdom: a small act of folly can outweigh much wisdom
alternatives: a little folly is more costly than wisdom and honor
decisions.reason: The word (*yaqar*) means heavy or precious. Here the little folly "weighs more" than wisdom and honor: it can undo them. The verse carries on the thought of 9:18, where one sinner destroys much good.

decisions.choice: make stink, make bubble: two verbs side by side, the oil stinks and ferments
decisions.reason: The two verbs stand together without "and", as often in vivid speech. The second means to bubble or pour out, as rotting oil does.

decisions.choice: the cluster of sayings
decisions.reason: Chapter 10 is mostly a collection of short sayings. Verses 1-4 and 8-20 are set in lines; verses 5-7, where Qoheleth reports what he has seen, are prose.

decisions.choice: so (B); In the same way (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make explicit that the second line is the lesson of the picture in the first.

source.text: לֵ֤ב חָכָם֙ לִֽימִינ֔וֹ וְלֵ֥ב כְּסִ֖יל לִשְׂמֹאלֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] heart of [the] wise [is] to his right, and [the] heart of [a] fool to his left.

en.L: The heart of a wise [one is] at {{gender:their|his}} right, \q but the heart of a fool at {{gender:their|his}} left.
en.B: The heart of the wise leans to the right, \q the heart of a fool to the left.
en.R: The heart of a wise person points the right way. \q The heart of a foolish person points the wrong way.

decisions.choice: right and left: the side of strength and favor, and the side of weakness
decisions.reason: The right hand was the hand of strength, skill and favor (Genesis 48:13-14; Psalm 16:8; 110:1). The left was the weaker side. The saying means that the wise person's mind leads to what is good and the fool's to what is bad.

decisions.choice: heart: mind and will
decisions.reason: As in 7:4, the heart is the inner person that decides where to go.

decisions.choice: fool (L, B); foolish person (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *kesil*: "fool" at Literal and Balanced, "foolish person" ("foolish people") at Readable.

decisions.choice: points the right way ... points the wrong way
alternatives: to his right ... to his left
decisions.reason: Readable says what right and left stand for (m1). In modern speech "left" and "right" can suggest politics, which is not meant.

source.text: וְגַם־בַּדֶּ֛רֶךְ כְּשֶׁסָּכָ֥להֹלֵ֖ךְ לִבּ֣וֹ חָסֵ֑ר וְאָמַ֥ר לַכֹּ֖ל סָכָ֥ל הֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: And also on the road, when the fool walks, his heart is lacking, and he says to all [that] [a] fool he [is].

en.L: And even on the road, when the fool walks, {{gender:their|his}} heart is lacking, \q and {{gender:they say|he says}} to everyone [that] {{gender:they are|he is}} a fool.
en.B: Even when fools walk along the road, they lack sense, \q and they show everyone that they are fools.
en.R: Even when foolish people are just walking down the road, it is clear that they have no sense. \q They show everyone how foolish they are.

decisions.choice: his heart is lacking: he lacks sense
decisions.reason: "Lacking heart" means lacking sense (Proverbs 6:32; 10:13).

decisions.choice: he says to everyone that he is a fool: he shows everyone his folly
alternatives: he says of everyone else that they are fools
decisions.reason: The fool's very behavior tells everyone that he is a fool. The words can also be read: "he says of everyone that they are fools", the fool thinking everyone else foolish. The first reading suits the saying better.

decisions.choice: fool: one without sense
decisions.reason: This word (*sakal*) is the fool of 7:17 and 10:14.

decisions.choice: fool (L, B); foolish (R)
decisions.reason: This word for fool (*sakal*) is rendered like *kesil*: "fool" at Literal and Balanced, "foolish person" at Readable.

decisions.choice: show
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say how the fool "says" it: by what he does (m2).

source.text: אִם־ר֤וּחַ הַמּוֹשֵׁל֙ תַּעֲלֶ֣ה עָלֶ֔יךָ מְקוֹמְךָ֖ אַל־תַּנַּ֑ח כִּ֣י מַרְפֵּ֔א יַנִּ֖יחַ חֲטָאִ֥ים גְּדוֹלִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: If [the] spirit of the ruler rises against you, your place do not leave; for calmness lays to rest offenses great.

en.L: If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, \q do not leave your place; \q for calmness lays great offenses to rest.
en.B: If the ruler's anger rises against you, \q do not leave your post, \q for calmness can lay great offenses to rest.
en.R: If someone in power becomes angry with you, \q do not walk away from your post. \q Staying calm can put even serious offenses to rest.

decisions.choice: spirit: anger
decisions.reason: The word (*ruach*) means spirit or temper; when it "rises" against someone it is anger (Judges 8:3).

decisions.choice: do not leave your place: do not walk out of your post in protest
decisions.reason: As in 8:3, leaving one's place before a ruler means quitting his service in anger. Staying is wiser.

decisions.choice: calmness: a gentle, steady manner
decisions.reason: The word (*marpe'*) can mean healing or calmness. Proverbs 15:4 uses it for a gentle tongue. A calm answer can settle a ruler's anger (Proverbs 15:1; 25:15).

decisions.choice: lays great offenses to rest: calms anger over great offenses
alternatives: keeps one from committing great offenses
decisions.reason: The words may mean that calmness settles the ruler's anger even over serious wrongs, or that calmness keeps the servant from committing serious wrongs, such as rebellion. The first fits the verse best.

decisions.choice: someone in power
decisions.reason: Readable uses a general phrase, since the ruler may be any person in authority.

source.text: יֵ֣שׁ רָעָ֔ה רָאִ֖יתִי תַּ֣חַת הַשָּׁ֑מֶשׁ כִּשְׁגָגָ֕ה שֶׁיֹּצָ֖א מִלִּפְנֵ֥י הַשַּׁלִּֽיט׃

records.literal_gloss: There is evil [that] I have seen under the sun, as an error that goes out from before the ruler:

en.L: There is an evil [that] I have seen under the sun, like an error that goes out from before the ruler:
en.B: There is an evil I have seen under the sun, the kind of error that comes from a ruler:
en.R: Here is something bad that I have seen in this world. It is the kind of mistake that comes from a ruler:

decisions.choice: an error: an unintended wrong, a blunder
decisions.reason: The word (*shegagah*) is the law's word for a sin committed without meaning to (Leviticus 4:2; Numbers 15:27). The ruler's mistake may not be deliberate, but it does harm.

decisions.choice: like an error: an error of a kind
decisions.reason: "Like" here means "the sort of thing that is": what follows is a kind of blunder made by those in power.

decisions.choice: verses 5-7 are Qoheleth's own observation
decisions.reason: "There is an evil I have seen under the sun" is Qoheleth's way of reporting what he has observed (5:12; 6:1). Verses 5-7 are set as prose; the sayings in lines resume at verse 8.

decisions.choice: under the sun (L, B); in this world (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for "under the sun" (see 1:3): kept at Literal and Balanced; Readable says "here on earth" or "in this world".

source.text: נִתַּ֣ן הַסֶּ֔כֶל בַּמְּרוֹמִ֖ים רַבִּ֑ים וַעֲשִׁירִ֖ים בַּשֵּׁ֥פֶל יֵשֵֽׁבוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Is set the folly in heights great, and [the] rich in [a] low place sit.

en.L: Folly is set in great heights, and [the] rich sit in a low place.
en.B: Folly is set in many high positions, while the rich sit in lowly places.
en.R: Foolish people are given important positions, while people of rank are given low ones.

decisions.choice: folly: foolish people, folly in person
decisions.reason: "Folly" stands for those who are foolish, as in 10:1. Fools are put in high office.

decisions.choice: the rich: people of standing and means
decisions.reason: Set against "folly", "the rich" here are people of rank and substance, those who would be expected to govern. Their place is taken by fools.

decisions.choice: great heights: high positions, or many high positions
decisions.reason: The words can mean "great heights" or "many high places". Either way they mean positions of power.

decisions.choice: people of rank
decisions.reason: Readable says what "the rich" stands for here (m2).

source.text: רָאִ֥יתִי עֲבָדִ֖ים עַל־סוּסִ֑ים וְשָׂרִ֛ים הֹלְכִ֥ים כַּעֲבָדִ֖ים עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: I have seen slaves on horses, and officials walking like slaves on the ground.

en.L: I have seen slaves on horses, and officials walking like slaves on the ground.
en.B: I have seen slaves on horseback, while officials go on foot like slaves.
en.R: I have seen slaves riding on horses while leaders walk on the ground like slaves.

decisions.choice: on horses: riding as a mark of high rank
decisions.reason: Horses belonged to kings and nobles (Esther 6:8-9; Jeremiah 17:25). Slaves riding while officials walk is the world upside down.

decisions.choice: slaves: people owned by others, the lowest in rank
decisions.reason: The word (*'eved*) is a slave or servant, one owned and not hired. Here it is the opposite of the officials.

decisions.choice: officials: princes, men of rank in the king's service
decisions.reason: The word (*sar*) is used for officials and princes, the ruling class (10:16-17).

decisions.choice: slaves (L, B, R)
decisions.reason: The project usually renders *'eved* "servant" at Balanced and Readable, but keeps "slave" where slavery itself is the point. Here the contrast is between the lowest and the highest in society, which "servant" would weaken.

decisions.choice: officials (L, B); leaders (R)
decisions.reason: The project's wording for *sar*: "officials" at Literal and Balanced, "leaders" at Readable.

source.text: חֹפֵ֥ר גּוּמָּ֖ץ בּ֣וֹ יִפּ֑וֹל וּפֹרֵ֥ץ גָּדֵ֖ר יִשְּׁכֶ֥נּוּ נָחָֽשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: [One] digging [a] pit into it will fall, and [one] breaking through [a] wall will bite him [a] snake.

en.L: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, \q and whoever breaks through a wall, a snake will bite {{gender:them|him}}.
en.B: Whoever digs a pit may fall into it, \q and one who breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
en.R: If you dig a pit, you may fall into it. \q If you break through a wall, a snake may bite you.

decisions.choice: whoever digs a pit will fall into it: a proverb also found in Proverbs 26:27
decisions.reason: Proverbs 26:27 and Psalm 7:16 use the saying of those who set traps for others and are caught in them. The word for "pit" here is a different one, found only here.

decisions.choice: will fall, will bite: the risks that come with any work
alternatives: the punishment that comes to those who plot harm
decisions.reason: In Proverbs the saying is about getting what one deserves. Here it is followed by quarrying and splitting wood (verse 9), which are ordinary work, so the point seems to be that every task has its dangers, and wisdom helps (verse 10). The verbs can be read as what will happen or what may happen. Both senses may be meant.

decisions.choice: a snake in a wall: snakes lived in the cracks of stone walls
decisions.reason: Field walls and house walls were built of loose stones, where snakes hid (Amos 5:19).

decisions.choice: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it
decisions.reason: Literal reuses the wording of Proverbs 26:27, since the saying is the same.

decisions.choice: may fall ... may be bitten (B); may fall ... may bite (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "may", since the verse is about risk (m2).

source.text: מַסִּ֣יעַ אֲבָנִ֔ים יֵעָצֵ֖ב בָּהֶ֑ם בּוֹקֵ֥עַ עֵצִ֖ים יִסָּ֥כֶן בָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: [One] quarrying stones will be hurt by them; [one] splitting logs will be endangered by them.

en.L: Whoever quarries stones will be hurt by them; \q whoever splits logs will be endangered by them.
en.B: Whoever quarries stones may be injured by them, \q and whoever splits logs is put in danger by them.
en.R: If you cut stones from a quarry, you may get hurt. \q If you split logs, you may be injured.

decisions.choice: quarrying stones and splitting logs: the heavy work of building
decisions.reason: Stone was cut and moved for building (1 Kings 5:31), and logs were split for building and fuel. Both were dangerous work (Deuteronomy 19:5).

decisions.choice: will be endangered: is put at risk
decisions.reason: The verb is rare. It most likely means to be in danger.

decisions.choice: may be injured ... is put in danger (B); may get hurt ... may be injured (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 8, Balanced and Readable speak of risk.

source.text: אִם־קֵהָ֣ה הַבַּרְזֶ֗ל וְהוּא֙ לֹא־פָנִ֣ים קִלְקַ֔ל וַחֲיָלִ֖ים יְגַבֵּ֑ר וְיִתְר֥וֹן הַכְשֵׁ֖רחָכְמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: If is blunt the iron, and he not [the] face has sharpened, and strength he must increase; and [the] gain of making succeed [is] wisdom.

en.L: If the iron is blunt, and {{gender:one|he}} has not sharpened [its] edge, \q then {{gender:one|he}} must use more strength; \q but the gain of giving success [is] wisdom.
en.B: If the ax is blunt and its edge is not sharpened, \q more strength must be used; \q but wisdom brings the gain of success.
en.R: If your ax is dull and you do not sharpen it, \q you have to work harder. \q But here is what good wisdom does: it helps you succeed.

decisions.choice: the iron: the iron head of an ax
decisions.reason: "Iron" stands for an iron tool, here the ax of verse 9 (Deuteronomy 19:5; 2 Kings 6:5).

decisions.choice: the gain of giving success is wisdom: wisdom makes the work succeed
alternatives: wisdom has the advantage of preparing (sharpening) beforehand
decisions.reason: The Hebrew of this verse is hard, and its words are rare. The general sense is clear: a dull ax needs more effort, and wisdom (like sharpening the ax first) brings success with less. The last line can be read as "wisdom is the advantage that brings success" or "wisdom has the advantage of setting things right".

decisions.choice: sharpened the face: sharpened the edge
decisions.reason: The "face" of a blade is its edge.

decisions.choice: gain (L, B); what good ... does (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *yitron* (see 1:3).

decisions.choice: ax
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the tool (m1).

source.text: אִם־יִשֹּׁ֥ךְ הַנָּחָ֖שׁ בְּלוֹא־לָ֑חַשׁ וְאֵ֣ין יִתְר֔וֹן לְבַ֖עַל הַלָּשֽׁוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: If bites the snake without charming, then there is no gain to [the] master of the tongue.

en.L: If the snake bites without charming, \q then [there is] no gain to the master of the tongue.
en.B: If the snake bites before it is charmed, \q there is no gain in being a charmer.
en.R: If a snake bites before it has been charmed, \q then the snake charmer's skill does no good.

decisions.choice: charming: calming a snake with chants
decisions.reason: Snake charmers used sounds and chants to control snakes (Psalm 58:6; Jeremiah 8:17). If the snake strikes first, the charmer's skill is wasted.

decisions.choice: the master of the tongue: the charmer, whose skill is in his words
decisions.reason: The phrase means a snake charmer, who works by speaking. It also prepares for verses 12-14, which are about what people say.

decisions.choice: skill used too late is no use
decisions.reason: Like verse 10, the saying is about timing: wisdom must be used at the right moment.

decisions.choice: gain (L, B); does no good (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *yitron* (see 1:3).

source.text: דִּבְרֵ֥י פִי־חָכָ֖ם חֵ֑ן וְשִׂפְת֥וֹת כְּסִ֖יל תְּבַלְּעֶֽנּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Words of [the] mouth of [a] wise [one are] grace, and [the] lips of [a] fool swallow him.

en.L: Words of a wise [one's] mouth [are] grace, \q but the lips of a fool swallow {{gender:them|him}} up.
en.B: The words of a wise person's mouth win favor, \q but fools are swallowed up by their own lips.
en.R: What wise people say wins them goodwill. \q But foolish people are destroyed by their own words.

decisions.choice: grace: favor, goodwill
decisions.reason: The word (*chen*) means grace or favor. The words of the wise are gracious, and they win favor for the speaker (Proverbs 22:11).

decisions.choice: the lips of a fool swallow him: a fool is ruined by his own words
decisions.reason: The fool's own lips devour him, as Proverbs 18:7 says: a fool's mouth is his undoing.

decisions.choice: fool (L, B); foolish people (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *kesil*: "fool" at Literal and Balanced, "foolish person" ("foolish people") at Readable.

source.text: תְּחִלַּ֥ת דִּבְרֵי־פִ֖יהוּ סִכְל֑וּת וְאַחֲרִ֣ית פִּ֔יהוּ הוֹלֵל֖וּת רָעָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] beginning of [the] words of his mouth [is] folly, and [the] end of his mouth [is] madness evil.

en.L: The beginning of the words of {{gender:their|his}} mouth [is] folly, \q and the end of {{gender:their|his}} talk [is] evil madness.
en.B: The words of their mouths begin with folly, \q and their talk ends in harmful madness.
en.R: What foolish people say starts out foolish \q and ends up as dangerous madness.

decisions.choice: evil: harmful, ruinous
decisions.reason: The word (*ra'ah*) here describes the result of the fool's talk: madness that does harm.

decisions.choice: beginning ... end: from start to finish
decisions.reason: The fool's talk is foolish from first to last, and it gets worse as it goes on.

decisions.choice: harmful (B); dangerous (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of evil is meant (m1).

decisions.choice: foolish people
decisions.reason: Readable names who is speaking: the fool of verse 12.

source.text: וְהַסָּכָ֖ל יַרְבֶּ֣ה דְבָרִ֑ים לֹא־יֵדַ֤ע הָאָדָם֙ מַה־שֶׁיִּֽהְיֶ֔ה וַאֲשֶׁ֤ר יִֽהְיֶה֙ מֵֽאַחֲרָ֔יו מִ֖י יַגִּ֥יד לֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And the fool multiplies words; not knows the human what will be, and what will be after him, who will tell to him?

en.L: And the fool multiplies words; \q {{gender:a person|man}} does not know what will be, \q and what will be after {{gender:them|him}}, who can tell {{gender:them|him}}?
en.B: A fool keeps on talking, \q though no one knows what is to come, \q and who can tell anyone what will happen after them?
en.R: Foolish people talk on and on. \q But no one knows what will happen. \q No one can tell anyone what will happen after they are gone.

decisions.choice: the fool multiplies words, though no one knows the future
alternatives: the second half quotes the fool's own words
decisions.reason: The fool talks a great deal, as if he knew what is coming. The rest of the verse answers him: no one knows. Some read the second half as the fool's own empty talk.

decisions.choice: no one knows what will be after him
decisions.reason: The words repeat 6:12 and 8:7. The future, and what happens after death, is hidden from all.

decisions.choice: fool (L, B); foolish people (R)
decisions.reason: This word for fool (*sakal*) is rendered like *kesil*: "fool" at Literal and Balanced, "foolish person" at Readable.

source.text: עֲמַ֥ל הַכְּסִילִ֖ים תְּיַגְּעֶ֑נּוּ אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־יָדַ֖ע לָלֶ֥כֶת אֶל־עִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] toil of the fools wearies him, who not knows to go to [the] city.

en.L: The toil of fools wearies {{gender:them|him}}, \q for {{gender:they do|he does}} not know [how] to go to [the] city.
en.B: The hard work of fools wears them out, \q for they do not even know the way to town.
en.R: Foolish people wear themselves out with their work. \q They do not even know how to find their way to town.

decisions.choice: not knowing the way to the city: complete ignorance of the obvious
decisions.reason: This seems to be a common saying for someone who cannot manage the simplest thing. The road to the city was the plainest of roads (Isaiah 35:8 speaks of a road where even fools will not go astray).

decisions.choice: fools ... him: each fool
decisions.reason: The Hebrew moves from plural "fools" to singular "him". Each fool is worn out.

decisions.choice: toil ... fools (L); hard work ... fools (B); work ... foolish people (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *'amal* and *kesil*.

source.text: אִֽי־לָ֣ךְ אֶ֔רֶץ שֶׁמַּלְכֵּ֖ךְ נָ֑עַר וְשָׂרַ֖יִךְ בַּבֹּ֥קֶר יֹאכֵֽלוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Woe to you, land, when your king [is a] youth, and your officials in the morning eat.

en.L: Woe to you, land, when your king [is] a youth, \q and your officials feast in the morning.
en.B: Woe to you, land, when your king is a boy \q and your officials feast in the morning!
en.R: How terrible it will be for you, land, \q when your king is just a boy \q and your leaders feast in the morning!

decisions.choice: woe to you: a cry of distress over the land
decisions.reason: The word here is a rare form of the cry of woe (also in 4:10). It warns of trouble to come.

decisions.choice: a youth: a boy, young and inexperienced; possibly a servant
decisions.reason: The word (*na'ar*) means a boy or young man, and also a servant (Genesis 22:3). Set against "a son of nobles" in verse 17, it may mean a king of low birth as well as a young one. Either way he is not fit to rule (Isaiah 3:4).

decisions.choice: feasting in the morning: indulgence when the day's work should be done
decisions.reason: The morning was the time for judging and governing (Jeremiah 21:12). Rulers who begin the day with feasting and drink neglect their duty (Isaiah 5:11).

decisions.choice: Woe to you (L, B); How terrible it will be for you (R)
decisions.reason: The project's wording for a woe aimed at others, as for *hoy* in Isaiah.

decisions.choice: officials (L, B); leaders (R)
decisions.reason: The project's wording for *sar*: "officials" at Literal and Balanced, "leaders" at Readable.

decisions.choice: feast
decisions.reason: The verb means to eat, but eating at the start of the day set against "at the proper time" (verse 17) means feasting.

source.text: אַשְׁרֵ֣יךְ אֶ֔רֶץ שֶׁמַּלְכֵּ֖ךְ בֶּן־חוֹרִ֑ים וְשָׂרַ֨יִךְ֙ בָּעֵ֣ת יֹאכֵ֔לוּ בִּגְבוּרָ֖ה וְלֹ֥א בַשְּׁתִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Happy [are] you, land, when your king [is a] son of nobles, and your officials at the time eat, for strength and not for drinking.

en.L: How blessed [are] you, land, when your king [is] a son of nobles, \q and your officials eat at the [proper] time, \q for strength and not for drinking.
en.B: How blessed you are, land, when your king is of noble birth, \q and your officials eat at the proper time, \q to gain strength and not to get drunk.
en.R: Life is good for a land \q whose king comes from a noble family \q and whose leaders eat at the right time, \q to be strong, not to get drunk.

decisions.choice: how blessed: how happy, how fortunate
decisions.reason: The word (*'ashre*) is the cry of good fortune that opens Psalm 1. It answers the "woe" of verse 16.

decisions.choice: a son of nobles: a king of noble birth, a free man
decisions.reason: The word means free-born, of noble family (1 Kings 21:8). Such a king has been raised to rule.

decisions.choice: for strength and not for drinking: to be strong, not to get drunk
alternatives: with self-control and not in drunkenness
decisions.reason: The word for strength can also mean self-control. Either way the officials eat to be fit for their work, not to get drunk.

decisions.choice: How blessed (L, B); Life is good for (R)
decisions.reason: The wording of Psalm 1:1 for *'ashre*.

decisions.choice: officials (L, B); leaders (R)
decisions.reason: The project's wording for *sar*: "officials" at Literal and Balanced, "leaders" at Readable.

source.text: בַּעֲצַלְתַּ֖יִם יִמַּ֣ךְ הַמְּקָרֶ֑ה וּבְשִׁפְל֥וּת יָדַ֖יִם יִדְלֹ֥ף הַבָּֽיִת׃

records.literal_gloss: Through double laziness sinks the rafter, and through lowering of hands leaks the house.

en.L: Through laziness the rafters sink, \q and through slack hands the house leaks.
en.B: Through laziness the roof beams sag, \q and through idle hands the house leaks.
en.R: When people are lazy, the roof sags. \q When they do not use their hands, the house leaks.

decisions.choice: laziness: great laziness, or the laziness of both hands
decisions.reason: The word has a dual ending, used for pairs. It may stress how great the laziness is, or it may point to the two idle hands of the second line.

decisions.choice: the roof beams and the house: a flat roof that needed constant care
decisions.reason: Houses had flat roofs of wooden beams covered with packed earth. They had to be repaired and rolled after the rains, or they leaked (Proverbs 19:13; 27:15).

decisions.choice: the house: perhaps also the land of verses 16-17
decisions.reason: Set between sayings about rulers, the neglected house may also picture a land whose rulers neglect it. The saying first means what it says.

decisions.choice: lowering of hands: slack, idle hands
decisions.reason: Hands that hang down are hands that do not work (Proverbs 10:4).

source.text: לִשְׂחוֹק֙ עֹשִׂ֣ים לֶ֔חֶם וְיַ֖יִן יְשַׂמַּ֣ח חַיִּ֑ים וְהַכֶּ֖סֶף יַעֲנֶ֥ה אֶת־הַכֹּֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: For laughter they make bread, and wine makes glad life, and the silver answers the all.

en.L: For laughter they make bread, \q and wine makes life glad, \q and silver answers everything.
en.B: Feasts are made for laughter, \q and wine makes life merry, \q and money answers every need.
en.R: People hold feasts to have fun, \q and wine makes life happy, \q and money seems to take care of everything.

decisions.choice: bread: a meal, a feast
decisions.reason: "Making bread" means preparing a meal (Ezekiel 4:15). Here it is a feast, as in verse 16.

decisions.choice: money answers everything: money meets every demand
alternatives: money is the answer to everything
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to answer. Here it seems to mean that money supplies whatever is wanted. A word from the same root means "business" (1:13), and some read: money keeps all occupied. After verses 16-17, the saying may describe the outlook of rulers who feast, not advice the book gives.

decisions.choice: they make: people, perhaps the feasting rulers of verse 16
decisions.reason: "They" has no stated subject. It may mean people in general or the officials of verse 16.

decisions.choice: money
decisions.reason: Silver was money (7:12).

decisions.choice: seems to take care of
decisions.reason: Readable adds "seems" because the saying may report an attitude rather than state a truth (m2).

source.text: גַּ֣ם בְּמַדָּֽעֲךָ֗ מֶ֚לֶךְ אַל־תְּקַלֵּ֔ל וּבְחַדְרֵי֙ מִשְׁכָּ֣בְךָ֔ אַל־תְּקַלֵּ֖ל עָשִׁ֑יר כִּ֣י ע֤וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֨יִם֙ יוֹלִ֣יךְ אֶת־הַקּ֔וֹל וּבַ֥עַל כְּנָפַ֖יִם יַגֵּ֥יד דָּבָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: Even in your thought [the] king do not curse, and in [the] rooms of your bed do not curse [the] rich; for [a] bird of the heavens will carry the voice, and [a] master of wings will tell [the] matter.

en.L: Even in your thought do not curse [the] king, \q and in the rooms of your bed do not curse [the] rich; \q for a bird of the heavens will carry the sound, \q and a master of wings will tell the matter.
en.B: Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, \q nor the rich even where you sleep, \q for a bird in the sky may carry off your words, \q and a winged creature may report what you said.
en.R: Do not curse the king, even in your thoughts. \q Do not curse rich people, even in your bedroom. \q A bird may carry your words to them, \q and something with wings may tell them what you said.

decisions.choice: your thought: your mind, your private thoughts
decisions.reason: The word usually means knowledge. Here it is what a person thinks privately, set beside the privacy of the bedroom.

decisions.choice: a bird will carry the sound: secrets get out
decisions.reason: The picture is like the saying "a little bird told me". Words spoken in private have a way of reaching the very people they were spoken against.

decisions.choice: the king ... the rich: those with power to punish
decisions.reason: As in verse 6, "the rich" are the powerful, set beside the king.

decisions.choice: a master of wings: a winged creature, a bird
decisions.reason: "Master" (*ba'al*) with a noun describes what a thing has; a "master of wings" is a creature with wings.

decisions.choice: may carry ... may report (B); may carry ... may tell (R)
decisions.reason: The verbs can be read as what will or may happen. Balanced and Readable give the warning as a real risk.
